Script:


OSCAR – THE INTERVIEW

Oscar: I can smell the blood. I can feel the warmness of it on my hands. And to know that that’s your fault, that that’s what you’ve done. And I understand the pain people feel, that loved her and miss her. I feel that same pain. I feel that same hate for myself. I feel that same difficulty in understanding this. And I look back and I think I always think – how did this possibly happen? I think how could this have happened? How could this have happened?

Leonard: I think this is a public relations exercise, and I think that if he would have given evidence that showed remorse, that showed that he had done some reflection, I think that it could have been mitigating. Look I’m not speaking from a legal point of view. But this case has had the biggest jury in history, and I’ve never seen so many unconvinced people.

Oscar: I’m hiding behind the toilet entrance wall. I can see the toilet door. I don’t know if it’s one person, all I know is that there is somebody in my house. And all of a sudden I hear a noise at the toilet.

Leonard: When he was talking about what happened on the night he was talking in the present tense. Everything else was in the past tense. He was actually describing it as if he was watching a movie in his head and saying what was happening in the present tense. And I found that pretty odd.

Oscar: I presumed it was the toilet door opening and before I knew it I’d fired 4 shots.

Sfx: Bang, bang, bang, bang.

Oscar: I opened the toilet door and immediately when I saw Reeva she was over the toilet. She's.. she’d slumped over the toilet. And I [breaks down], at that point I knew that I'd killed her. I knew that she was dead. And I went down on my knees and pulled her onto me. (Cries)
And I thought Reeva had started breathing, so I had my fingers in her mouth and I was trying to give her mouth to mouth, but there was so much blood.
[sobbing, Oscar walks out

Greenland: His version to me now was utterly convincing. It had all the marks of authenticity, so to me as a judge it has the hallmarks of truth. But truth from where? Is this a truth that has been produced – and Leonard will help us with this – by the power of the mind after 3 years? Because I also know that happens. Or is it the actual truth?
Oscar: I don't know, you can ask yourself a million times, why, why didn't i just close the door before I went to bed? Why didn't Reeva close the door? Why when she got up to go to the toilet just tell me? Why didn't she shout at me from the toilet and all these things. I can’t say, why did she do them, she didn't do anything wrong. But it's difficult.
Bongani: The tears, the sense of anguish that you saw that Oscar has in that interview, did that move you in anyway?
Many: From my point of view, if I was sitting in the matter and presiding in the matter, it’s got to have some impact on you.
Oscar: They try and say that I broke down the door with the cricket bat standing on my stumps…I can’t even hold a cricket bat up if I don’t have my arms to balance.
Mark: Are you aggressive to women?

OSCAR: No

MARK: Have you ever been violent to women?

OSCAR: No, not at all.

John: He was only asked one difficult question and it pertained to why somebody according to others was a bit of a hothead would be allowed to own a weapon?

MARK: Clearly an indication that was coming through … that you are this hotheaded person, who display signs of violence and shouldn't carry a gun…

OSCAR: I don't even have an answer to that.

Leonard: Well I think because he’s not authentic as a person and he’s staging his version, he’s actually managing perceptions all the time as he’s speaking. So when he’s in a situation where he doesn’t now what the right response is to get the image across that he’s trying to, he almost goes blank and he’s stuck.

MWT: Some would say, well you should spend a very long time in jail, you took someone's life.

OP: I can’t disagree with that … At times I don't feel like I should have the right to live for taking somebody else's life. What is difficult is dealing with this charge of murder.

Bongani: Even now he talks about it being a charge of murder, he’s not talking about it being a conviction, and yet it is quite clearly now a conviction of murder. Does that surprise you?

Leonard: Not at all, because he’s never really owned the consequences of his behaviour.

Oscar: The day before we started the trial on the 2nd March 2014 I sat with my lawyers and I said to them, whatever happens I will spend – the maximum for culpable homicide is 10 years – I said to them, ‘I will spend 10 years in jail for taking Reeva’s life, for culpable homicide but I won’t spend a day in jail for murdering anyone.’

Greenland: He takes this rather pious stance that he’s prepared to be something of a martyr and go to jail even for 10 years for culpable homicide, but not for having murdered Reeva, completely discounting the fact that on his own version he was executing another human being.

Oscar: I don't want to go back to jail; I don't want to have to waste my life sitting there. If I was afforded the opportunity of redemption I would like to help the less fortunate like I had in my past. I would like to believe that if Reeva could look down upon me that she would want me to live that life.

Greenland: She’s got to sentence him on the basis that he executed an intruder, that’s it stripped down, shorn of everything, because that’s exactly what he did.

OP: I don't argue with anyone that feels that they should lock me up and throw the key away. Reeva was a fantastic person, but if their premise is based on the fact that I took her life intentionally, which has not been found … then it's a very sad thing. To think that society would want to do that I had only contributed positively - I'd like to believe - to people's lives before this tragedy happened.
